title: AustralianSuper given sector's first AAA rating
full_text:
AustralianSuper has become the first superannuation provider to achieve an AAA credit rating from ratings agency Moody's, surpassing both the Victorian and Queensland governments in a major coup for the country's largest pension fund.
The fund, which has $438 billion in assets under management, hired Citi to provide advice on achieving the rating.
The rating is expected to save AustralianSuper more than $250 million in transaction costs between now and 2035, when it is forecast to manage more than $1 trillion in assets for more than 5 million members.
Between 30 and 40 people worked across the fund's Melbourne and London offices to secure the rating.
The score puts AustralianSuper on par with the federal government's credit rating, and ahead of certain state governments such as Victoria and Queensland (AA2 and AA1, respectively). It is a better rating than that held by Commonwealth Bank (AA2) and the other major banks.
Moody's said the rating reflects its "very conservative financial policies; its large, highly diversified investment portfolio; and [a] member demographic that cannot be easily replicated".
"The fund has a market-leading share in memberships across almost all age groups and a particularly strong presence among younger workers, which supports durable contribution growth," wrote Moody's Investors Service senior credit officer Daniel Yu.
"Over the past decade, the fund has consistently retained more than 90 per cent of assets after member outflows while, on average, inflows have exceeded outflows by more than 200 per cent."
AustralianSuper chief liquidity officer Chandu Bhindi led the internal effort since February to get the rating.
Bhindi has previously floated getting rid of long-standing rules that prevent it and other major pension funds from borrowing money or issuing debt, but the project was designed with the nearer term goal of lower costs for AustralianSuper when trading derivatives within the Basel IV regime that govern the latest global banking reforms.
The rules put new capital requirements on parties and counterparties using derivatives, increasing the amount of capital they have to hold at-risk based on their credit rating to ensure broader system stability.
With an AAA rating, AustralianSuper will hold less capital at risk than other derivatives traders.
Derivatives exposures were less than 1 per cent of AustralianSuper's assets, Moody's said, and it expected "the fund to remain unleveraged, given statutory restrictions on borrowings".
The ratings agency noted its "increasingly sophisticated liquidity management" mitigated the risk of member withdrawals on the broader portfolio.
AustralianSuper expects other funds to follow suit but, because of strict rules around marketing, it cannot use the rating in its advertisements.
AustralianSuper chief executive Paul Schroder said that the rating "should make a meaningful difference to reducing the costs of investments and transactions, particularly as we grow our global investment footprint".
"AustralianSuper uses derivatives and other financial instruments to help manage risk and ensure access to markets in all conditions. AustralianSuper is the first non-government-owned pension fund globally to receive an AAA long-term issuer rating from Moody's."
Nine Entertainment Co.
